spec.cue: Most monkeys and apes see colour, but less sharply than you, and the sharp middle is small.

PRIMATE_LM.note: a two-cone mapping used for the dichromatic and owl monkey cases; the app's reading

M.note: the app's two-cone reading; the records show three cone classes in most monkeys and one or two in others

cpd.note: the app's pick, between the cited macaque and marmoset figures; the sharpest cited figure for a monkey is about 26 and the cited figures for many other primates are lower

fovea.note: no record gives the size of the sharp middle in scale terms; the app's guess

gain.note: no dim-light ratio is cited for these animals

sat.note: no measure of colour strength is cited; the app's guess

rows: Most monkeys and apes have three kinds of colour sensor. Owl monkeys and bushbabies have only one kind of cone, so they see no colour, and some New World monkeys have two.
A rhesus monkey reaches about 26 cycles per degree and a marmoset is estimated near 30, against a person's 60. Mouse lemurs are far less sharp, near 4 to 5.
Owl monkeys are nocturnal and see without colour. Marmosets, rhesus monkeys, capuchins and chimpanzees are active by day.
Owl monkeys have only a rudimentary fovea, while squirrel monkeys and macaques have a clear fovea with dense cones at its centre.

The picture is blurred to about 12 cycles per degree, a little more than a bushbaby would show and well below the monkeys' best, and the sharp middle is drawn at a scale of 2.2. These are the app's choices and the records give no exact figure.

claims.how: The app picked 12 cycles per degree as a point between the cited macaque figure of 26.3 (R7) and the 21.4 cycles per degree worked from 1.4 arc minutes (R12), with the marmoset's estimate of 30 (R2) as a ceiling; this is worked out and invented, and graded g.

quotes.quote: achieving the maximum acuity level assessed (26.3 c/deg) by 7 weeks of age for most monkeys
Visual acuity in a normal stumptail macaque is 1.4 minutes of arc-similar to man's.
up to 30 cycles/deg in monkeys and humans
The foveal acuity predicted by the Nyquist limits set by the cone mosaic (30 c/deg) is in agreement with behavioral measures of visual acuity.

rows: A scorpion has a median pair of eyes in the middle of the carapace and lateral eyes along each side. Lateral eye pairs number five in many buthid scorpions, and median and lateral eyes together give a view that reaches all round the body.
Scorpion eyes peak in blue light near 470 nm and in green light near 525 nm. The view keeps these colours and mutes red, which the records say scorpions are weakly sensitive to.
Scorpion eyes respond to starlight levels of light, and scorpions are nocturnal, so the picture lifts dim scenes.
A scorpion finds much of its food and its way with the hairs and slits on its legs, the pectines and the palps. The camera records none of these, so the picture shows only what the eyes would.
No record gives how much detail a scorpion sees. The view is coarse, with the middle a little sharper, and still things fade partly so that movement and light stand out.
Vibrations through sand and air, and the touch of the legs, carry much of what a scorpion knows, and the screen shows none of them.

claims.how: Both records give a 360 degree field of view, so the whole-animal field is set to 360.

quotes.quote: scorpions can apparently see 360° around their body
Together, the two eyes have a 360 deg field of view

rows: The sharp front eyes of most jumping spiders carry two colour pigments, one ultraviolet near 360 nanometres and one green near 530 nanometres. The picture keeps two colour channels and no red.

A typical principal eye resolves about 3.8 cycles per degree, and its field is only about 5 degrees wide. A person is about 30 and sees a much larger sharp patch, so this window is small and coarse by comparison.
The side eyes resolve about 1.3 cycles per degree at best. Together they cover nearly the whole circle around the spider, so the soft picture reaches behind you.
The side eyes behave as though blind to stationary objects, and a small movement is enough to send the spider turning toward it. The sharp eyes then look closely.
The sharp eyes sweep side to side across a target, with a period of one to two seconds and never under 2 degrees. They also twist about 20 to 30 degrees each way.
After the sharp eyes inspect a place, the side eyes stop noticing movement there for about five seconds.

The app chose to apply the side eyes' sharpness and field to the whole picture, to fade colour outside the middle, to let still things fade outside the middle, to draw the ultraviolet channel from the camera's blue, and to place the window at the centre of the screen.

claims.how: The record gives 1.3 cycles per degree for the antero-lateral eye of Evarcha blancardi.
Both records give a combined field of view of 360 degrees for the secondary eyes of salticids.
The record gives a visual field of around 5 degrees for each principal eye.
The record gives 3.8 cycles per degree for Phidippus johnsoni principal eyes.
The amplitude 2 degrees comes from R134 and the period 1.5 seconds is the middle of R129's 1 to 2 seconds.
5 seconds times 1000 gives 5000 milliseconds.

spec.cue: The world holds one tone and the field is very wide. A horizontal stripe across the middle stays sharpest.

fov.note: a squid four weeks old; the app chose this animal to stand for the group

cpd.note: the squid value; an octopus is near 12 and a cuttlefish near 8, and the app chose one value for the group

sheen.note: no reflective layer has been found in cephalopod eyes, so the app switches the sheen off

M.note: one visual pigment peaking near 485 nanometres gives a single tone; the mapping is the app's

single_pigment_485.note: one pigment, so the picture keeps brightness and loses hue

cpd.note: worked out from the squid sharpness and the density of receptors in the central stripe of an octopus retina

rows: A squid resolves about 6.6 cycles per degree, a cuttlefish about 8 and an octopus about 12, against a person's 30. The picture is softened to the squid value.

These animals hold one visual pigment, with its peak near 480 nanometres in octopus, near 492 in a cuttlefish and near 500 in a squid. Tests found that an octopus cannot tell colours apart. The picture keeps brightness and loses hue.

Young oval squid see 295 to 329 degrees around them, and the uniocular field of one cuttlefish eye spans 253 degrees across. The picture is squeezed toward 322 degrees, the field of a squid four weeks old.

An octopus packs about 55,000 receptors per square millimetre into a horizontal stripe across the middle of the retina, against 18,000 to 22,000 at the edge. A horizontal band of the picture is kept sharper, by a figure worked out from those densities.
An octopus pupil is round in darkness and closes to a horizontal slit in bright light. It closes within about a second and shrinks to about a tenth of its dark area.
No reflective layer behind the retina has been found in any cephalopod, so the eye shows no sheen.
Octopuses notice tiny differences in the plane of polarized light, a contrast that a person cannot see at all. The picture leaves it out for now.

The squid value of 6.6 cycles per degree, the field of a four week old squid, the single 485 nanometre tone, the horizontal slit pupil, the sharpness of the stripe and the switched off sheen are the app's own settings, placed inside the measured ranges.

claims.how: The field of a squid 28 days old is 322 degrees in the table row.
The squid acuity is 6.56 cycles per degree.
Names the matrix built from the single 485 nanometre pigment peak that both records give.
